target.title: Towards Unified Neural Decoding with Brain Functional Network Modeling

read.pdf: PDF not supplied; read text-extracted captions for Fig. 1–4 and Fig. S1–S5 and all of Tables S1–S5; plotted figure values are not present in text.txt

entries.text: MIBRAIN is presented as a unified, multi-individual framework that builds a whole functional brain-network model from intracranial recordings across subjects.
entries.condition: Authors' stated methodological contribution.

entries.text: The claimed novelty includes self-supervised regional prototypes and a temporal/regional fusion mechanism for a common representation across subjects.
entries.condition: Pretraining and representation-learning design.

entries.text: The cohort comprised 11 epilepsy patients, all native Mandarin speakers; five were female and six male.
entries.condition: sEEG cohort; five female and six male; all native Mandarin speakers with intact language functions as later stated.
entries.quote: This study enrolled a total of 11 participants with five females and six males.

entries.text: The reading stimulus set contained 407 unique Mandarin characters spanning the reported syllable combinations.
entries.condition: Audible and silent character-articulation tasks; 407 unique monosyllabic characters.
entries.loc: Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: The label inventory is described as 23 distinct initials in Results; Discussion specifies 21 initial consonants plus the finals i and u, so the 23-class scope includes those two finals.
entries.condition: The paper's wording differs between its Results and Discussion descriptions of the phoneme inventory.

entries.text: The authors contrast the 407-character stimulus set with a Mandarin vocabulary exceeding 50,000 characters; the experiment did not decode that full vocabulary.
entries.unit: Mandarin characters in the broader vocabulary
entries.condition: Context only; experimental stimuli were the 407-character set.
entries.loc: Results: MIBRAIN enables generalized neural decoding

entries.text: Compound vowel finals including ou and ao were omitted; the proof-of-concept task focused on initial consonants with two selected simple finals.
entries.condition: Phoneme-articulation classification scope.

entries.text: Participants read each character 3–5 times; a complete 407-character set was one session, containing either audible or silent trials in random order.
entries.condition: Count varied with individual enrollment duration; each complete session was one articulation mode.
entries.loc: Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: Each reading trial used 0.8–1.2 s preparation, 2 s articulation, and 0.5–1.0 s rest.
entries.condition: Character reading task, both articulation modes.
entries.loc: Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: The online test set comprised 69 characters, selected as three characters beginning with each reported initial phoneme.
entries.condition: Online decoding fatigue-reduction test set; three selected for each of 23 initials/classes as described in Methods.
entries.loc: Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: Offline within-subject evaluation selected seven samples per initial class per subject (161 test samples), with remaining recordings assigned to training and validation.
entries.condition: 23 classes; accuracy evaluated per subject; multi-subject training integrated data from multiple subjects.
entries.quote: for each subject, we randomly selected seven samples from each initial class, yielding a total of 161 test samples for evaluation, with the remaining recordings used for training and validation.

entries.text: Offline audible evaluation covered 11 participants; offline silent evaluation covered five participants.
entries.condition: Offline decoding-accuracy comparisons; silent-task participation was lower.

entries.text: The authors report that single-subject and multi-subject MIBRAIN outperform Brant, BrainBERT, and chance on audible and silent tasks, with the stated exception of participant 4.
entries.condition: Offline; both articulation modes; all participants except participant 4; comparisons include MIBRAIN variants and chance baseline.
entries.loc: Results: MIBRAIN enables generalized neural decoding

entries.text: Multi-subject MIBRAIN is reported to have higher offline accuracy than single-subject MIBRAIN for most participants.
entries.condition: Offline audible and silent phoneme articulation decoding.
entries.loc: Results: MIBRAIN enables generalized neural decoding

entries.text: Reported offline multi-subject over single-subject accuracy improvements were 8.08% and 6.83% for audible, and 5.10% and 4.97% for silent articulation, for participants 10 and 11 respectively.
entries.condition: Offline decoding; participants 10 and 11; audible and silent articulation; multi-sub versus single-sub. The prose does not label each of the four values by participant-mode cell beyond its listed order.
entries.quote: 8.08% and 6.83% for audible articulation, and 5.10% and 4.97% for silent articulation
entries.loc: Results: MIBRAIN enables generalized neural decoding

entries.text: Participants 3, 4, and 8 had lower decoding performance; the authors attribute this to dialectal pronunciation and phoneme confusions.
entries.condition: Offline performance; reported examples include n/l and alveolar s versus retroflex sh confusions.
entries.loc: Results: MIBRAIN enables generalized neural decoding

entries.text: Online experiments involved participants 10 and 11; each completed two randomized trials per mode with 10-minute rests, then one hour of free practice and four additional sessions (two per mode).
entries.unit: trials per mode; minutes rest; hour practice; post-practice sessions
entries.condition: Real-time online audible and silent decoding; post-practice sessions comprised two per articulation mode.
entries.loc: Results: Real-time decoding of MIBRAIN; Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: The authors report above-chance online decoding before practice without subject-specific calibration or training, and higher multi-subject than single-subject performance across reported conditions.
entries.condition: Participants 10 and 11; online audible and silent decoding; pre-practice and post-practice.

entries.text: After practice, reported online multi-subject over single-subject accuracy improvements were 3.62%, 2.90%, 7.97%, and 4.35% for participants 10 and 11 and audible/silent modes as listed by the authors.
entries.condition: Post-practice online decoding; participants 10 and 11; audible and silent articulation; multi-sub versus single-sub. The prose does not label each value by participant-mode cell beyond its listed order.

entries.text: Online decoding accuracy increased after free practice; the authors interpret post-practice performance as a more accurate measure of model capability.
entries.condition: One-hour self-paced free-practice session; both articulation modes.

entries.text: The data-scaling analysis trained 11 models per test participant, incrementally using data from one through all 11 participants; enrollment order determined the sequence.
entries.unit: models per test participant; training participants
entries.condition: Online test participants 10 and 11; all test-participant recordings reserved as test data in the described scaling setup; order was not exhaustively enumerated.
entries.loc: Results: Integrating more participants’ data improves decoding; Methods: Experimental setup

entries.text: The authors report an initial accuracy decline when fewer than three additional participants were added; for audible decoding, improvement became significant at six or more additional participants for both test participants.
entries.unit: additional training participants; reported significance threshold
entries.condition: Online scaling analysis for participants 10 and 11; significance statement applies to audible articulation; additions follow enrollment order.
entries.loc: Results: Integrating more participants’ data improves decoding

entries.text: The authors call conclusions about decoding scalability in the silent task preliminary because fewer participants completed that task.
entries.condition: Online scaling analysis; silent articulation.
entries.loc: Results: Integrating more participants’ data improves decoding

entries.text: Unseen-subject evaluation used leave-one-subject-out validation: train on the other participants and evaluate on all data from the held-out participant.
entries.condition: Both audible and silent articulation; subject-level held-out data; evaluation on each unseen participant.
entries.quote: we trained MIBRAIN models on neural data aggregated fr om all participants except one (the held-out test subject), and we then evaluated decoding performance using data from this unseen subject.

entries.text: For held-out subjects, decoding accuracy was below the full-data model but remained significantly above the chance baseline; silent-task performance was closer to the full-data result than audible-task performance.
entries.condition: Leave-one-subject-out offline decoding, audible and silent articulation.
entries.loc: Results: MIBRAIN generalizes to unseen subjects

entries.text: Unseen-subject decoding uses participant-specific embeddings and requires ensemble-based prediction, which the authors identify as a limitation for efficiency and unified encoding.
entries.condition: Unseen-subject inference; majority voting across the existing subjects' encoders/predictions.
entries.quote: our current approach employs participant-specific embeddings that necessitate ensemble-based decoding for predictions on unseen subjects.
entries.loc: Discussion; Methods: Neural Decoding on Unseen Subject

entries.text: Cross-task online decoding was lower than task-specific decoding but significantly above baseline; the audible-model-to-silent direction performed better than silent-model-to-audible.
entries.condition: Participants 10 and 11; online; models trained on audible or silent data; cross-decoding in both directions.
entries.loc: Results: Cross-decoding between audible and silent articulation

entries.text: The authors report that representations imputed for removed brain regions correlate strongly with the corresponding directly recorded representations.
entries.condition: For each participant, one recorded region was removed at a time; predicted representations were compared with the corresponding region and other regions using correlations.
entries.quote: We observed strong similarity between predicted and actual neural representations for each removed region, as indicated by high correlation values along the diagonal of the correlation matrix (Fig. 3a).
entries.loc: Results: Imputed brain regions correlate with ground-truth representations

entries.text: Decoding using only imputed regions exceeded chance for audible trials except participants 4 and 8 (reported P < 0.001 for the other participants); silent decoding was also above chance.
entries.condition: Offline decoding using solely imputed brain-region representations; audible and silent tasks.
entries.quote: in all participants except participants 4 and 8 during audible decoding.
entries.loc: Results: Neural decoding with imputed regional representations

entries.text: The Discussion claims that decoding with imputed representations exceeds state-of-the-art methods based on direct recordings, without giving a numerical comparison there.
entries.condition: Discussion-level comparative claim; imputed-region decoding versus methods based on direct recordings.
entries.quote: neural decoding using solely MIBRAIN's imputed neural representations achieves performance exceeding state- of-the-art methods based on direct recordings.

entries.text: Audible regional-contribution analysis covered 500 ms before through 500 ms after annotated articulation onset; the authors report SFG contribution as early as 500 ms before onset.
entries.unit: milliseconds relative to audible articulation onset
entries.condition: Audible articulation only; onset identified from audio by expert linguistic annotation.
entries.loc: Results: Dynamic contribution of brain regions; Discussion

entries.text: The authors did not perform the same contribution analysis for silent articulation because onset could not be exactly identified and aligned without audio cues.
entries.condition: Silent articulation; visual-cue reaction-time and pronunciation variability also complicate alignment.

entries.text: MIBRAIN is used to infer task-related functional relationships and region collaboration; the authors interpret the resulting regional patterns as evidence of broad network interactions.
entries.condition: Group-level analysis of phoneme articulation; associations include reported IFG–SFG and IFG–SMG collaboration.

entries.text: sEEG acquisition used 2,000 Hz for participants 1–4 and 2,048 Hz for participants 5–11; signals were downsampled to 512 Hz after filtering.
entries.condition: Participants 1–4 used Neurofax EEG-1200; participants 5–11 used Natus Quantum LTM Amplifier.
entries.loc: Methods: Recording and preprocessing of neural signal

entries.text: Neural signals were low-pass filtered at 200 Hz, notch filtered at 50 and 100 Hz, and downsampled to 512 Hz; channels were removed after manual quality review.
entries.condition: Applies to neural recordings before channel selection and model input.
entries.loc: Methods: Recording and preprocessing of neural signal

entries.text: Channel selection compared mean 4–150 Hz PSD during articulation versus rest using paired t-tests and Benjamini–Hochberg correction; significant channels met corrected P < 0.05.
entries.condition: Cortical channels only; white matter and visual-cortex channels excluded.
entries.quote:
values in the 4–150 Hz band between articulation and resting conditions via paired t-
tests. We applied Benjamini-Hochberg corrections to control the false discovery rate34, 
retaining channels that showed significant differences (corrected P < 0.05).
entries.loc: Methods: Recording and preprocessing of neural signal

entries.text: Audio was recorded at 44.1 kHz; neural/audio contamination was checked using randomly selected 10-minute intervals.
entries.condition: Directional microphone; audio and neural signals stored separately.
entries.loc: Methods: Recording and preprocessing of audio signal

entries.text: Supplementary acoustic-contamination significance testing compared observed diagonal values against nulls from 10,000 shuffled matrices.
entries.condition: Supplementary Fig. S2; contamination matrices for each participant.

entries.text: Three phonetics experts independently labeled articulation for audio segments; PRAAT aligned labels to neural recordings and marked onset timestamps.
entries.condition: Audio segments; onset timestamps used for audible articulation analyses.
entries.loc: Methods: Recording and preprocessing of audio signal

entries.text: Whole-network pretraining used AdamW, learning rate 1×10⁻⁵, cosine annealing, weight decay 0.005, batch size 16 times the number of training subjects, and 1,000 epochs.
entries.unit: learning rate; weight decay; batch size; epochs
entries.condition: Self-supervised whole functional network prototyping; β1=0.9 and β2=0.999.

entries.text: Supervised decoding used AdamW, learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, cosine annealing, weight decay 0.001, and 200 fixed epochs; baseline training followed the cited authors' setups.
entries.condition: Neural decoding stage; momentum factors β1=0.9 and β2=0.999.

entries.text: Neuro-embedding encoders use two 1-D convolutional blocks, kernels 7 and 5, strides 4 and 2, dropout 0.1, and embedding dimension 32; the temporal encoder uses four convolutional blocks and reduces temporal length by 16.
entries.unit: blocks; kernels; strides; dropout; dimensions; temporal blocks; reduction factor
entries.condition: Architecture described for regional encoders and temporal CNN.
entries.quote: Each block comprised a one -dimensional convolutional layer followed by batch normalization, with leaky rectified linear units as the activation function.

entries.text: The region-attention encoder contains two MHSA blocks, each with an FFN ratio of four; the decoding head is MLP-based.
entries.condition: Neural decoding stage.

entries.text: Raw audio and neurophysiological data cannot be publicly distributed under the stated clinical ethics guidelines; data may be requested from the corresponding author under confidentiality restrictions.
entries.condition: Source data underlying figures are stated to be provided with the paper.

entries.text: The cohort consists exclusively of epilepsy patients with intact language functions; the authors call for future evaluation in patients with diverse language disorders.
entries.condition: Clinical generalization beyond the 11-participant cohort is untested.

entries.text: The authors identify mispronunciation as a considerable source of decoding-accuracy loss and note its prevalence among potential neuroprosthesis users.
entries.condition: Speech-prosthesis relevance; especially patients who may benefit from speech neuroprostheses.

entries.text: The authors limit the demonstrated task scope to phoneme articulation and identify general-purpose modeling as future work.
entries.condition: Current experiments use Mandarin phoneme articulation rather than a broad set of cognitive or communication tasks.

entries.text: No random seeds or number of independently repeated model-training runs are reported for the stochastic training, masking, and sample-selection procedures.
entries.condition: Evaluation reproducibility; no seed/repetition count stated in the methods or results.
entries.quote: we randomly selected seven samples from each initial class

entries.text: The train/validation split of the recordings left after selecting offline test samples is not specified, and validation data or criteria used for checkpoint/model selection are not identified.
entries.condition: Offline evaluation; the paper only says remaining recordings were used for training and validation.

entries.text: The paper does not say whether feature/channel selection and self-supervised prototype pretraining excluded the held-out offline test samples; selection appears in preprocessing before the experimental split is described.
entries.condition: Potential selection-data overlap; no train-only channel-selection protocol is reported.
entries.quote: retaining channels that showed significant differences (corrected P < 0.05).
entries.loc: Methods: Recording and preprocessing of neural signal; Experimental setup

entries.text: The primary offline subject-level split uses test and training/validation samples from the same participant; the separate LOSO experiment holds out an entire subject.
entries.condition: Main offline comparisons are not subject-disjoint; LOSO is the subject-disjoint evaluation.

entries.text: Whether the Brant and BrainBERT pretraining corpora included data from the evaluated participants or overlapping recordings is not stated.
entries.condition: Baseline pretraining data provenance and participant overlap.
entries.loc: Results: MIBRAIN enables generalized neural decoding

entries.text: The paper reports filtering, channel selection, and batch normalization within the encoder but does not describe input-signal amplitude normalization or per-subject normalization.
entries.condition: Neural signal preprocessing before model input; normalization beyond the specified network batch normalization.
entries.loc: Methods: Recording and preprocessing of neural signal; Framework architectures

entries.text: Although chance-level baselines are shown and discussed, their numerical value and construction are not specified.
entries.condition: Classification over the reported phoneme classes; chance baseline used in offline figures and narrative comparisons.
entries.quote: compared to Brant, BrainBERT, and a chance -level baseline.

entries.text: The exact train/test conditions, hyperparameter-selection procedure, and data split for Brant and BrainBERT comparisons are not detailed beyond referring to the original authors' experimental setups.
entries.condition: Baseline comparison against Brant and BrainBERT.

entries.text: No use-time language model, external lexical decoder, or other language-model aid is specified; the described prediction head is MLP-based.
entries.condition: Phoneme-initial classification; statement is limited to aids described in the paper.

entries.text: During free practice, the display showed “Correct” when at least one model predicted correctly; otherwise it displayed the top three predictions ranked by confidence.
entries.unit: predictions displayed on an incorrect result
entries.condition: Real-time free-practice feedback; multiple parallel models could provide predictions.
entries.loc: Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: The paper describes displaying incorrect top-three predictions but does not specify a user correction action or whether corrections are collected and used to update decoding.
entries.condition: Online interaction during practice and testing.
entries.loc: Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: The study reports real-time streaming to a server but gives no end-to-end decoding latency or deployment throughput measurement.
entries.condition: Online evaluation; experiments were run using PyTorch on NVIDIA H800 GPUs.
entries.loc: Results: Real-time decoding of MIBRAIN; Methods: Experimental setup

entries.text: The authors propose potential clinical relevance for patients with severe impairments or limited recording opportunities, but this application is prospective rather than evaluated in the cohort.
entries.condition: Experiments were performed in epilepsy patients with intact language functions, not the proposed impaired clinical population.

entries.text: MIBRAIN's pretraining uses masked autoencoding to learn regional prototypes by reconstructing signals from within-subject and functionally related cross-subject information.
entries.condition: Whole functional network prototyping; pretext objective reconstructs intracranial recordings.
entries.quote: To achieve this, we introduce a masked autoencoding-based pretext task.

entries.text: For online phoneme-decoding evaluations, the multi-subject model was trained using data collected from all 11 subjects; participant identities therefore occur in the training cohort and online test cohort.
entries.condition: Online evaluation uses live data from participants 10 and 11; the paper does not identify the session-level separation between training recordings and live test recordings.
entries.quote:
For online phoneme decoding 
evaluations, data collected from all subjects were used for model training (MIBRAIN-
multi-sub).

entries.text: The paper does not specify whether the online test sessions, including the post-practice sessions, are excluded at the recording/session level from the all-subject training data.
entries.condition: Online decoding by participants 10 and 11; training pool is stated to contain data from all subjects, but trial/session partitioning is not detailed.
entries.quote: For online phoneme decoding evaluations, data collected from all subjects were used for model training (MIBRAIN- multi-sub).
entries.loc: Methods: Experimental setup; Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.text: Table S1 reports participant ages of 14–35 years, 8–13 implanted electrodes, and 30–88 selected channels per participant.
entries.condition: Ranges computed across all 11 participants in Table S1.

entries.text: The exact neural epoch boundaries used for classification relative to the visual cue, articulation onset, and the two-second articulation interval are not specified.
entries.condition: The task timing is described, but the precise input-window start/end used for offline and online decoding is not.
entries.loc: Methods: Task of phoneme articulation decoding

entries.quote: significantly above chance level even before the practice session, despite the absence of any subject specific calibration or training

entries.text: No absolute decoding accuracy (percent correct) for MIBRAIN, Brant, BrainBERT or chance is given in the text or supplementary tables; absolute values appear only as bars in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3; the gains (8.08%, 7.97% etc.) are not stated as percentage points or relative.
entries.condition: Whole text and Tables S1-S5 checked (Tables S2-S5 are stimulus lists).
